messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Karim's Vigil

Karim had been a firefighter for twelve years, and in that time he had learned to move through crisis with the steadiness of someone trained to trust his own reflexes. At thirty-seven, married to Yasmin for nine years, he had built a life that felt solid—the kind of life his parents, who had emigrated from Lebanon before he was born, had worked hard to make possible for him. But the man who showed up to the firehouse now was not the same one who had left it on a Tuesday morning in early March.

The stalking had begun without announcement. Karim first noticed the bicycle in early February—a man he didn't recognize, riding slowly past his house on Maple Street at odd hours. The man never approached, never spoke. He simply appeared: at the corner when Karim left for work, parked outside the station one afternoon, waiting on the sidewalk when Karim and Yasmin returned from the market. When Karim tried to speak to him, the man would cycle away quickly, only to reappear the next day. Karim had called the police, filed reports, changed his route home. Nothing stopped it. The man's face—lean, expressionless, eyes that seemed to catalogue Karim's movements—had burned itself into Karim's mind with the intensity of a threat he could see but not fully understand or control.

Then, on that Tuesday in March, the man had been waiting outside the station at dawn. When Karim stepped outside to begin his shift, the man stood directly in his path, close enough that Karim could see the detail of his worn jacket. "I know where you live," the man had said quietly. "I know where your wife goes." Karim had moved toward him, but the man had melted backward into the pre-dawn darkness, and by the time Karim reached the street, he was gone. The police arrested him three days later after Yasmin spotted him outside their bedroom window. The man was charged; he was held. But something in Karim had not been arrested with him.

In the weeks that followed, Karim's body became a instrument of vigilance. He could not enter a room without cataloguing its exits—the door to the kitchen, the window in the break room, the side entrance at the station. His colleagues had begun to notice. During calls, he was sharp, reliable, but back at the station, something had shifted. He would sit in the common area with his back to the wall, watching the faces of the firefighters around him, searching for the subtle signs of threat he had learned to read in the stalker's blank expression. When a truck rumbled past the station or a siren wailed in the distance, his entire body would tense. Loud, unexpected sounds made his heart race in a way that embarrassed him—a grown man, trained for emergencies, jumping at noise.

What frightened Karim most was the conviction that had settled into his chest: that he had become weak. A weak man would have been followed. A weak man would be afraid now. He had come to believe that the stalking had exposed something true about him, something permanent. He was not the steady, reliable person he had always thought he was. The evidence was in how he scanned rooms, in how he could not sleep without checking the locks twice, in how the sight of a bicycle—any bicycle, ridden by anyone—could send him into a state of panic so overwhelming that he had to step away from whatever he was doing and breathe until the world stopped spinning.

Yasmin had suggested, gently, that he talk to someone. She had noticed that he was withdrawing, that he had stopped attending the community dinners they used to enjoy, that he flinched when she touched him unexpectedly. He had resisted at first. But three weeks ago, when he found himself unable to describe to his captain why he had reacted so violently to a fellow firefighter's joke about being followed, when the memory had crashed over him without warning and left him standing in the apparatus bay unable to speak, unable to articulate what was happening inside him, he had finally called. Now, sitting in a therapist's office, Karim was trying to find the words for what it meant to have been changed by someone else's gaze, and to believe that the change was permanent.
